Answer: D) Kongamato

The kongamato, whose name means "overwhelmer of boats," is a pterosaur-like cryptid reported from the Jiundu Swamp in the Mwinilunga district of western Zambia, and from Angola and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Frank Melland wrote about it in his 1923 book In Witch-Bound Africa, describing a reddish flier with a 4 to 7 foot wingspan said to capsize boats from below, and Kaonde people shown a pterosaur picture in his book said it looked exactly like one. Accounts add smooth featherless skin and a toothy beak, while skeptics point to shoebill or saddle-billed storks and Ivan T. Sanderson favored a giant bat.

How'd you do?
posts.headline: Answer: D) Kongamato

posts.text:
Route 150, Kensington, New Hampshire, about three miles south of Exeter. September 3, 1965.

It's around 2 in the morning, and 18-year-old Norman Muscarello is walking home along the highway. He's three weeks away from leaving for the Navy, he's just sold his car, and he's been hitchhiking back from his girlfriend's house in Amesbury, Massachusetts. At that hour there's hardly any traffic.

Then he sees five bright red lights flashing in the distance. At first he figures it's a police car or a fire engine. It isn't. The lights are hovering just above the trees, bathing a field and two houses in brilliant red. He puts the object at 80 to 90 feet across, and it makes absolutely no sound. When it starts moving toward him, he dives into a ditch. He pounds on a farmhouse door yelling for help, and the family inside later admits they heard him but were too frightened to open it.

He flags down a car and gets a ride to the Exeter police station, pale and shaking. Officer Eugene Bertrand drives him back out. Earlier that night, Bertrand had stopped for a frightened woman who said a huge object with flashing red lights had followed her car for about 12 miles.

Out in the field, horses start neighing and kicking the barn, dogs bark and howl, and an object rises slowly from the trees. Bertrand calls it a huge dark object "as big as a barn," with red lights flashing in sequence as it rocks back and forth. He drops to one knee and draws his revolver, then thinks better of it. Officer David Hunt arrives and watches it too. When a B-47 bomber flies over soon after, Hunt says there was no comparison.

The Pentagon blames stars and planets twinkling in a temperature inversion. The officers push back, and in January 1966 the Air Force writes that it has been unable to identify the object. Skeptics later suggested a KC-97 refueling tanker, but Muscarello insisted for the rest of his life that what he saw was real.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exeter_incident
posts.headline: Route 150, Kensington, New Hampshire, about three miles south of Exeter. September 3, 1965.

posts.text:
Bladenboro, Bladen County, North Carolina. December 1953 to January 1954.

On December 29, 1953, something kills a dog in Clarkton, about eight miles from Bladenboro. Witnesses describe the animal as sleek, black, and about five feet long.

Two nights later, on New Year's Eve, two dogs belonging to a Bladenboro resident are found dead near their kennels, "torn into ribbons and crushed." The owner says it killed one dog at 10:30, then came back and carried the body off, and at 1:30 in the morning it came back again for the other one.

More dogs die over the next week. A pet rabbit turns up cleanly decapitated, and a goat is found with its head flattened. When one dog is autopsied, it reportedly has barely two or three drops of blood left in it, and the newspapers start calling it a vampire beast.

Nobody can agree on what it is. One local says it had a face exactly like a cat, only bigger than any cat he'd ever seen, with a long tail. Others compare it to a bear or a panther. A boy says it made a noise like a baby crying on his porch. On January 5, a woman says "a big mountain lion" ran straight at her and only turned away when she screamed. Hunters from Wilmington track it three miles around the swamp and find claw prints at least an inch long, and along a creek bank there are two sets of tracks, one smaller, like it has a mate or young nearby.

By January 6, more than 800 people with guns and dogs are combing the swamps, and officials shut the hunt down as too dangerous. On January 13, a farmer shoots a bobcat caught in a steel trap in Big Swamp, and Mayor Woodrow Fussell announces the beast is dead. Plenty of people doubt a bobcat could have done all that. Fussell, who ran the town theater and booked a movie called The Big Cat right in the middle of the scare, later said he thought it was a hoax and that "a little publicity never hurts a town."

Bladenboro still holds a Beast Fest every year, with the beast as its mascot.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beast_of_Bladenboro
posts.headline: Bladenboro, Bladen County, North Carolina. December 1953 to January 1954.

posts.text:
Whaley House, San Diego Avenue, Old Town San Diego, California. Built 1857.

In 1852, a man named James "Yankee Jim" Robinson is convicted of attempted grand larceny for trying to steal a boat, and he's hanged from a gallows off the back of a wagon on this very lot. One of the people watching that day is a merchant named Thomas Whaley. A few years later, he buys the land anyway.

Whaley designs a two-story brick Greek Revival house, the oldest brick structure in Southern California, and moves his family in on August 22, 1857. According to the San Diego Union, soon after they move in, heavy footsteps start moving through the house. Whaley says they sound like the boots of a large man, and he finally decides they belong to Yankee Jim.

The house sees plenty of grief. Baby Thomas Jr. dies of scarlet fever at 18 months. Daughter Violet, heartbroken after a disastrous marriage, dies by suicide in 1885 at just 22. Youngest daughter Lillian lives there until her death in 1953, convinced Yankee Jim never left.

Visitors and staff still report glimpses of the Whaleys themselves: Thomas on the upper landing in a frock coat and pantaloons, his face turned away, and Anna in the downstairs rooms and the garden. In 1964, Regis Philbin, filming for a local San Diego morning show, says he noticed "something filmy white" on the wall. He flipped on his flashlight and found nothing but a portrait of Anna Whaley. Years later he still said, "there was something going on in that house."

Travel Channel's America's Most Haunted went further, calling it the most supernatural home in the United States.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaley_House_(San_Diego,_California)
posts.headline: Whaley House, San Diego Avenue, Old Town San Diego, California. Built 1857.

posts.text:
Lakewood, Colorado, just west of Denver. September 8, 2026.

It's about 7:05 in the evening and a Lakewood resident is sitting outside, just watching the clouds. Then they notice something that doesn't feel right. The birds and the animals around them have gone unusually quiet.

A bright object appears in the southern sky, almost like it's settling into view, and starts moving north. The witness gets it on video. It looks silver, metallic, but parts of it seem to turn see-through, and at other moments it looks less like a craft and more like a bright light. Even its shape won't hold still.

It glides smoothly at changing speeds, no zigzags, no sudden turns, and there's no sound at all. No engine, no propeller, nothing. They put it at bigger than an airliner.

Then, about thirty seconds in, it's just gone. It doesn't slip behind a cloud. It doesn't fade off into the distance. It simply stops being there.

The witness files the whole thing with the National UFO Reporting Center as sighting 200790, footage and all, and that strange silence before it showed up is the one detail they made sure to include.

Source: https://garnerreport.com/the-vanishing-object-over-lakewood/
posts.headline: Lakewood, Colorado, just west of Denver. September 8, 2026.

posts.text:
Diamond Bay, Lake Norfork, nine miles east of Mountain Home, Baxter County, Arkansas. September 28, 2026.

Donald Anderson is 70 years old and has been hunting his whole life. On this Monday morning he's bowhunting alone on the south main lake point in Diamond Bay, hardwoods and cedar running right down to the water. It's 7:30, about 60 degrees, sunny, and there isn't a breath of wind. He says you could hear a pin drop.

Then something howls out of the trees. Fifteen seconds later, it howls again.

He knows coyotes. He knows wolves. He's heard both all his life, and this was neither. The only place he's ever heard a sound like it is on the Bigfoot shows, in recordings people have made out in the woods.

He reports it to the BFRO that same day. Founder Matthew Moneymaker writes back that the big, slow, lake-like rivers along the Missouri and Arkansas border are full of deer and full of Bigfoot reports, and this side of Lake Norfork is exactly the kind of place where howls like these get heard this time of year. They carry a long way, he says, and there's a good chance they come again. So if you're anywhere near Diamond Bay, keep your phone ready and record.

Source: https://www.bfro.net/GDB/show_report.asp?id=82619
posts.headline: Diamond Bay, Lake Norfork, nine miles east of Mountain Home, Baxter County, Arkansas. September 28, 2026.

Have you heard of Gog and Magog?

Top 5 things to know about the Bible's end-times enemies:

1) In Ezekiel 38, Gog is a prince and Magog is his land, and the prophecy says Gog will lead a great alliance of nations against a restored Israel and be destroyed.

2) Genesis 10 names Magog as a son of Japheth and a grandson of Noah, and the historian Josephus believed Magog's descendants were the Scythians.

3) Revelation 20 says that when Satan is released after a thousand years, he will gather the nations in the four corners of the Earth, Gog and Magog, for a final battle, in number like the sand on the seashore.

4) By the Roman period a legend said Alexander the Great built gates to hold them back, and the Quran tells of Yajuj and Majuj, walled off by the righteous ruler Dhu'l-Qarnayn.

5) The names may have given rise to Gogmagog, a legendary British giant, and a later folk version split him into two giants named Gog and Magog, the figures London's Guildhall statues came to be identified with.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gog_and_Magog
posts.headline: Have you heard of Gog and Magog?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Bear Lake Monster?

Top 5 things to know about the serpent of the Utah-Idaho border:

1) The legend took off with an 1868 Deseret News article by settler Joseph C. Rich, who wrote that local settlers swore they had seen a serpent-like creature the Indians called a water devil.

2) Accounts vary, describing a serpent with legs about eighteen inches long, at least forty to fifty feet in length, faster than a locomotive, with a head like a cow, otter, crocodile or walrus without the tusks.

3) In 1874, LDS bishop William Budge wrote that he and two friends saw its furry face, flat and very wide between the eyes, with large blue eyes and ears like a horse's.

4) Brigham Young wanted to find out whether it was an honest tale of a serpent or only a fish story, and he even sent a large rope to Paris, Idaho to help capture it.

5) Twenty-six years after his articles, Rich admitted it had all been a wonderful first-class lie, yet sightings kept coming, and the last reported one was in June 2002.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Lake_monster
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Bear Lake Monster?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Headless Horseman?

Top 5 things to know about the rider who lost his head:

1) Headless riders have appeared in European folklore since the Middle Ages, sometimes carrying their heads and sometimes missing them altogether, maybe still searching for them.

2) Ireland's version is the dullahan, a headless demonic fairy who rides with his head under his arm and wields a whip made from a human corpse's spine, and when he calls out a name, that person dies.

3) In Germany's Rhineland, headless horsemen were said to kill just by touching their victims, wandering the earth as revenants until they had atoned for their sins.

4) Washington Irving's 1820 story The Legend of Sleepy Hollow may have been inspired partly by a rumored headless corpse found after the Revolutionary War Battle of White Plains, and there is a record of a Hessian soldier beheaded by a cannonball in that battle.

5) In southern Texas, stories of El Muerto have circulated since the mid-1800s, a headless rider who dangles his head from his saddle while his horse strikes lightning from its hooves.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headless_Horseman
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Headless Horseman?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Witch of Endor?

Top 5 things to know about the medium who called up a prophet's ghost:

1) In 1 Samuel 28, King Saul faces the assembled Philistine army and gets no answer from God through dreams, prophets, or the Urim and Thummim, even though he had already expelled the necromancers from Israel.

2) Saul disguises himself and crosses enemy lines to find a medium living at Endor, and when she refuses, citing his own royal ban on sorcery, he assures her she will not be punished.

3) The Hebrew calls her a woman who possesses an ov, a word some scholars link to a ritual pit for summoning the dead, and the Greek Septuagint calls her a belly-talker, an ancient term for a spirit medium.

4) She says she sees elohim rising from the ground, the word usually translated as gods, then describes an old man wrapped in a robe, and Saul bows down to a spirit he cannot see himself.

5) The spirit, whether Samuel himself or something impersonating him, warns that Israel's army will be defeated and that Saul and his sons will be with him tomorrow, and the next day Saul falls on his own sword.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witch_of_Endor
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Witch of Endor?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Pukwudgie?

Top 5 things to know about the little wild men of the New England woods:

1) The Pukwudgie is a mischievous or menacing dwarfish human-like creature of Native American lore, best known today from the folklore of the Wampanoag people of Massachusetts.

2) In their native form they are said to stand no more than knee-high, about two to three feet tall, with gray skin and very large noses, ears and fingers, and they can appear and disappear at will.

3) They are shape-shifters said to turn into cougars or quilled porcupines, and Wampanoag warnings say a disrespected Pukwudgie may fire poisoned arrows, lure people to their deaths in the forest, push them off cliffs, or kidnap children.

4) In Wampanoag myth they started out as well-meaning helper spirits who kept bungling things, until they turned so menacing that the giant Maushop gathered them up and swung them around, scattering them across New England.

5) The name comes from an Ojibwe tale published by Henry Rowe Schoolcraft in 1839 and made famous by Longfellow's The Song of Hiawatha in 1855, and a 1906 history of Middleboro, Massachusetts moved the story to Assawompset Pond.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pukwudgie
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Pukwudgie?

posts.text:
Answer: C) Wampus Cat

The wampus cat is a cat-like creature of American folklore with roots in Cherokee mythology and Appalachian legend, usually described as a large dark-furred feline with glowing green or yellow eyes, big claws and a scream like a cougar. Some versions give it six legs instead of four, and a 1936 Knoxville News-Sentinel description gave it a body 15 or 20 feet long with eyes like small moons. In the 1930s it was blamed for killing livestock in the Piedmont of North Carolina, and today it is the mascot of schools like Conway High School in Arkansas.

How'd you do?
posts.headline: Answer: C) Wampus Cat

posts.text:
Kecksburg, Pennsylvania, about 30 miles southeast of Pittsburgh. December 9, 1965.

At about 4:43 in the afternoon, a large, brilliant fireball streaks over the Detroit and Windsor, Ontario area. People in six U.S. states and Canada report it. Hot metal debris is reported over Michigan and northern Ohio, along with grass fires and sonic booms around Pittsburgh, and the FAA gets 23 reports from pilots.

In the village of Kecksburg, people report wisps of blue smoke, vibrations and a "thump," and say something from the sky has crashed in the woods. The Greensburg Tribune-Review reports the area is immediately sealed off on the order of U.S. Army and State Police officials. When troopers and Air Force personnel search the woods, they find "absolutely nothing," and a later edition runs the headline "Searchers Fail to Find Object."

Experts at the time call it a meteor. But in 1990, Unsolved Mysteries airs local residents saying they found an object in the woods shaped like an acorn, about as large as a Volkswagen Beetle, bearing writing like Egyptian hieroglyphs, and that it was removed in a secret military operation. John Hays, a boy of 10 at the time, says he saw a flatbed truck coming out of the site carrying something "the size of a VW."

In 2005, NASA says experts examined metal fragments from the area and found they came from a Soviet satellite, but the records were lost. After reporter Leslie Kean sues under the Freedom of Information Act, a court orders a search, and a NASA official testifies that two boxes of papers from the time are missing.

People still call it Pennsylvania's Roswell.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kecksburg_UFO_incident
posts.headline: Kecksburg, Pennsylvania, about 30 miles southeast of Pittsburgh. December 9, 1965.

posts.text:
Fulk Lake, near Churubusco, Indiana. 1948 to 1949.

Back in 1898, farmer Oscar Fulk claims he has seen a giant turtle living in the seven-acre lake on his farm. He tells others about it, then eventually lets the matter drop.

Nearly half a century later, in July 1948, Churubusco residents Ora Blue and Charley Wilson are fishing the same water, by then known as Fulk Lake, when they see a large turtle they estimate at about 500 pounds. The farm now belongs to Gale Harris, and he and others say they see it too. The turtle gets a name, Oscar, after the farm's original owner.

In early 1949, a UPI reporter from Fort Wayne sends the story out over the wire, and the whole country takes notice. Crowds of sightseers descend on the Harris farm until local authorities call in the state police to handle the traffic.

Harris goes all in. With help from Orville Bright and Kenneth Leitch, he tries to drain the lake by pumping its water into an area closed off by a dam. When the lake is nearly empty, the dam breaks and the water comes right back. In March 1949 a deep-sea diver is lined up, but the wrong equipment is delivered and the dive is abandoned. Life Magazine photographer Mike Shea takes 299 photographs. None of them are usable.

Oscar is never captured. Churubusco still celebrates Turtle Days every June, with a parade, a carnival and turtle races.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beast_of_Busco
posts.headline: Fulk Lake, near Churubusco, Indiana. 1948 to 1949.

posts.text:
112 Ocean Avenue, Amityville, Long Island, New York. December 1975 to January 1976.

On November 13, 1974, Ronald DeFeo Jr. shoots and kills six members of his family inside this big Dutch Colonial house on a canal. Thirteen months later, George and Kathy Lutz buy it for a bargain $80,000 and move in on December 18, 1975, with Kathy's three children and their dog, Harry. Much of the DeFeo family's furniture is still in the house.

According to the Lutzes' account in Jay Anson's 1977 book, a priest blessing the house that first afternoon hears a masculine voice demand that he "get out." By mid-January the family goes through a final night they call too frightening to describe. On January 14, 1976, after 28 days, they flee and leave all of their possessions behind. The mover who comes the next day reports nothing unusual.

In March 1976, Ed and Lorraine Warren investigate with a TV crew, and one infrared photo allegedly shows a "demonic boy" with glowing eyes at the foot of the stairs.

Skeptics push back hard. DeFeo's defense lawyer, William Weber, writes in People magazine, "I know this book is a hoax. We created this horror story over many bottles of wine." Later owner James Cromarty lives there ten years and says nothing weird ever happened, except for people coming by because of the book and the movie. George Lutz maintains it was mostly true.

The book sells around 10 million copies, and the 1979 film makes those two eye-like attic windows famous.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Amityville_Horror
posts.headline: 112 Ocean Avenue, Amityville, Long Island, New York. December 1975 to January 1976.

posts.text:
Pleasantville, Ewing and Winslow Township, New Jersey. Reported August to September 2026.

New Jersey 101.5's Lou Russo goes digging through the National UFO Reporting Center and finds more than a dozen sightings filed by Garden State residents since the beginning of August.

In Pleasantville, one witness watches a giant sphere flying horizontally, a massive eclipse shape giving off an orange glow.

In Ewing, someone sees mist or fog hanging in the sky with a big light in front of it and two more lights inside. The front light gets brighter, and the fog keeps changing shape the longer they watch.

And in Winslow Township, a driver looks out the front windshield and sees a white, cigar-shaped object following a plane. Within four or five minutes the object vanishes, but the plane is still right there.

Russo admits he's a UFO believer, and he doesn't think all of it can be blamed on SpaceX or a local airport. Maybe it's nothing, he writes. But imagine if it's not.

Source: https://nj1015.com/nj-ufo-update-september-2026/
posts.headline: Pleasantville, Ewing and Winslow Township, New Jersey. Reported August to September 2026.

posts.text:
Skookumchuck Reservoir, outside Tenino, Thurston County, Washington. May 18, 2024.

Five adults and three children are camping by the Skookumchuck Reservoir dam, private land behind three locked security gates that you can only reach if someone you know works for the company. Not long after they go to bed, a woman in her tent hears what she thinks is one of the men getting up to pee. Then it walks across the front of her twelve-foot-wide tent, about five feet away, in just a few long strides, and she knows right away it is not human.

She grabs her pistol and listens. For about 45 minutes it moves around the camp in a slow, steady rhythm, from the picnic table to the ice chest and grill, around the fire pit, over to the vehicles, always pausing near the food. Then a two-year-old starts crying in another tent. The footsteps march over and circle that tent at least three times, then stop dead in front of it. The other woman sets off her car alarm. It doesn't run. It walks past one last time, steps over a four-foot wire fence and snaps branches into the woods.

BFRO investigator Scott Taylor interviews her by phone. She tells him it took three steps to cross the tent, a 48-inch stride that is outside the human range, and she sends photos of wide, flat possible footprints.

Source: https://www.bfro.net/GDB/show_report.asp?id=82506
posts.headline: Skookumchuck Reservoir, outside Tenino, Thurston County, Washington. May 18, 2024.

posts.text:
Have you heard of Nimrod?

Top 5 things to know about the Bible's mighty hunter king:

1) Genesis 10 names Nimrod as the son of Cush, grandson of Ham, and great-grandson of Noah, calling him a mighty one in the earth and a mighty hunter before the Lord.

2) Genesis 10:10 says the mainstays of his kingdom were Babel, Uruk, Akkad and Calneh in the land of Shinar, and Micah later calls Assyria the land of Nimrod.

3) The Bible never says he built the Tower of Babel, but Josephus, the Talmud and later midrash make him the leader of its builders.

4) Josephus describes him as a bold man of great strength of hand who turned the government into tyranny and vowed to build a tower too high for floodwaters to reach.

5) Medieval tradition remade him as a giant. Dante chains him among the giants at the edge of Hell, and Hungarian legend calls him Nimród the Giant, forefather of the Hungarians.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nimrod
posts.headline: Have you heard of Nimrod?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Kraken?

Top 5 things to know about the sea monster that swallowed ships:

1) The kraken is a legendary sea monster of enormous size said to appear in the Norwegian Sea off the coast of Norway, usually pictured as something like a gigantic octopus or squid.

2) It was first described in a Norwegian glossary by Christen Jensøn in 1646, and its name comes from a Norwegian word for a crooked, overgrown tree, a fitting picture for twisting arms.

3) Bishop Erik Pontoppidan popularized it in his natural history of Norway in 1752 and 1753, writing that it could be mistaken for a cluster of small islands with fish swimming between them.

4) Pontoppidan also passed along the claim that if its arms laid hold of the largest man-of-war, they would pull it down to the bottom.

5) Many think the legend grew from real giant squid, which may reach about thirty-four feet long, and Victor Hugo and Jules Verne later carried the monster into famous fiction.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kraken
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Kraken?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Bell Witch?

Top 5 things to know about Tennessee's most famous haunting:

1) The legend centers on farmer John Bell Sr. and his family along the Red River near present-day Adams, in Robertson County, Tennessee, from 1817 to 1821.

2) It begins when John Bell sees a strange dog-like creature that vanishes when he fires at it, and soon the house fills with knocking, gnawing on the beds, chains dragging across the floor, and sheets pulled off sleeping children.

3) The invisible entity speaks, once claiming to be "Old Kate Batts' witch," and torments the youngest daughter, Betsy, who is slapped, pinched and stuck with pins.

4) In Martin V. Ingram's 1894 book, a vial of poison is found after John Bell fails to wake, and the witch claims she gave it to him.

5) Tales say Andrew Jackson's wagon froze in place on the way to the farm, though researchers find no evidence he ever visited, and today the Bell Witch Cave keeps the legend alive.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_Witch
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Bell Witch?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the cherubim?

Top 5 things to know about the Bible's most mysterious guardians:

1) Cherubim are the most frequently mentioned heavenly creatures in the Hebrew Bible, with the Hebrew word appearing 91 times, yet their role is never fully explained.

2) Their first appearance is Genesis 3:24, where God places cherubim and a flaming sword that turns every way at the east of Eden to guard the way to the tree of life.

3) From Ezekiel's vision of four living creatures came the classic image of a cherub with four faces, a lion, an ox, a human and an eagle, plus two pairs of wings and feet like a bull's hooves gleaming like polished brass.

4) Golden cherubim faced each other with their wings meeting over the mercy seat of the Ark of the Covenant, and Solomon's Temple held two that stood ten cubits high.

5) Scholars link them to winged guardian figures of the ancient Near East like the Assyrian lamassu, and the chubby baby cherubs of Western art came much later, borrowed from the Cupid-style putto.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherub
posts.headline: Have you heard of the cherubim?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Yeti?

Top 5 things to know about the Abominable Snowman of the Himalayas:

1) The Yeti is a large, hairy, ape-like creature said to live in the Himalayan mountains, usually described as walking upright and covered in brown, grey, or white hair.

2) The name traces to Tibetan words for rocky place and bear, and Tibetan lore describes three kinds, from the fifteen-foot, black-furred Nyalmo down to the small, reddish Rang Shim Bombo.

3) The nickname Abominable Snowman dates to the 1921 British Everest reconnaissance, when Calcutta newspaper writer Henry Newman mistranslated the Sherpa word metoh as filthy and turned it into abominable.

4) In 1951 Eric Shipton photographed huge footprints in the snow at about twenty thousand feet near Everest, and in 1954 a Daily Mail expedition gathered hairs from a supposed Yeti scalp kept at Pangboche monastery.

5) Sir Edmund Hillary's 1960 to 1961 Silver Hut expedition borrowed another scalp from Khumjung monastery for testing, and mountaineer Reinhold Messner later argued the Yeti is really a Himalayan bear that can walk upright.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeti

2026-10-05 15:20 ET
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Yeti?

Answer: A) Jackalope

The jackalope is the antlered jackrabbit of the American West. In the 1930s Douglas Herrick and his brother, hunters who learned taxidermy by mail order, grafted deer antlers onto a jackrabbit and sold the first one for ten dollars to the La Bonte Hotel in Douglas, Wyoming. Horned hare legends go back centuries, and researchers think rabbits with the Shope papilloma virus, which grows horn-like tumors, may have inspired some of them.

How'd you do?

posts.text:
A ranch near Corona, New Mexico, and the town of Roswell. June to July 1947.

Rancher W. W. "Mac" Brazel finds tinfoil, rubber, tape and thin wooden beams scattered across several acres of the ranch he manages. With no phone or radio, he has no idea the country is caught up in a flying disc craze. On July 5 his uncle suggests the debris could be from a "flying disk." The next day Brazel drives to Roswell and tells Sheriff George Wilcox, who calls Roswell Army Air Field, home of the 509th Bomb Group. Major Jesse Marcel and Captain Sheridan Cavitt go back with him to gather the material.

On July 8, base public information officer Walter Haut issues a press release saying the military has recovered a "flying disc." The story makes international headlines and is retracted within a day, when General Roger Ramey's press conference calls the material a weather balloon. Brazel still tells reporters he is sure it was not a weather observation balloon.

In 1978, Marcel claims the balloon story was a cover, and the 1980 book The Roswell Incident launches decades of crashed saucer theories. In the 1990s the Air Force ties the debris to Project Mogul, a top-secret balloon program built to detect Soviet nuclear tests.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roswell_incident

posts.text:
Fouke, Miller County, Arkansas. May 1971.

Bobby and Elizabeth Ford have lived in their house for less than a week, and for several nights they have heard something moving around outside late at night. On May 2, 1971, Elizabeth is sleeping on a couch when something she first thinks is a bear reaches through a screen window. Bobby and his brother Don chase it away and fire several shots. They believe they hit it, but no blood is found. Searchers turn up three-toed footprints near the house, scratch marks on the porch, and damage to a window and the siding.

Reports describe a large, hairy biped about seven feet tall and 250 to 300 pounds, with a terrible skunk and wet dog odor and bright red eyes the size of silver dollars. On May 23, three people report an ape-like creature crossing U.S. Highway 71. A Little Rock radio station posts a $1,090 bounty, and Miller County Sheriff Leslie Greer puts a temporary no guns policy in place for public safety.

An archaeologist calls the tracks a likely hoax, but the creature sticks. The 1972 film The Legend of Boggy Creek carries the Fouke Monster to drive-ins across the country.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fouke_Monster
posts.headline: Fouke, Miller County, Arkansas. May 1971.

posts.text:
284 Green Street, Brimsdown, Enfield, London, England. August 1977 to 1979.

Single mother Peggy Hodgson calls the Metropolitan Police to her rented council house, saying she has watched furniture move and that two of her four children have heard knocking on the walls. A police constable reports seeing a chair wobble and slide, and says he could not determine the cause.

The activity centers on sisters Janet, eleven, and Margaret, thirteen. Over eighteen months, more than thirty people, including neighbors, paranormal investigators and journalists, say they see heavy furniture move on its own, objects thrown across rooms, and the girls seeming to levitate. Many hear and record knocking and a gruff voice. Investigators Maurice Grosse and Guy Lyon Playfair believe at least some of it is genuine, and Ed and Lorraine Warren visit too.

Skeptics push back hard. A video camera catches Janet bending spoons, and the sisters admit to pranking some of it. Then a BBC series reveals that when the gruff voice of "Bill" was played on an LBC radio show, a listener identified it as his late father, William Charles Wilkins, who had lived in the house and died in a chair downstairs in 1963.

The case later inspires The Conjuring 2.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enfield_poltergeist
posts.headline: 284 Green Street, Brimsdown, Enfield, London, England. August 1977 to 1979.

Haywood County, Tennessee, north of Brownsville, looking northwest toward Halls. Reported September 30, 2026.

Mickey Utley, host of the paranormal and extraterrestrial talk show The Suppressed Signal on WTBG, is out on a really quiet, really dark night when he notices something like a bright star sitting low on the horizon. Then it starts fading in and out. On his footage, what looks like a plane soars across the night sky, vanishes without a trace, then reappears moments later.

He runs and gets his wife because he doesn't want to be the only one to see it. She goes out and, as he puts it, her jaw hits the ground for about ten seconds. When they come back out, the lights are gone.

Utley keeps alerts on several apps for satellites and spacecraft, including the Space Station, and he says none of them went off. Starlink didn't go off either. No thunderstorms, nothing around, he says, just crazy lights all over the place. He is also an amateur drone pilot and believes drones can be ruled out.

According to the National UFO Reporting Center, it would be the sixth UFO reported in the Brownsville area since 2000, and the first since 2023.

Source: https://www.wbbjtv.com/2026/10/01/radio-host-shares-possible-ufo-sighting-with-wbbj/

Washita River near Silo, northwest of Durant, Bryan County, Oklahoma. February 24, 2026.

Around five in the evening, a family of three drives over a hill at the end of Star Road and comes up on the Washita River. Across the water, something tall is walking across a powerline easement. It sees them come over the hill and stops.

Katy gets out of the truck, shaking. When the figure stands up and heads for the woods, she hollers as loud as she can. It stops, turns and looks back for maybe a second, then disappears into the trees. The whole thing lasts about fifteen seconds. She puts it at seven to eight feet tall, with dark brown hair that has a red glow in the sun going down behind it. Her husband and stepson see it too.

BFRO investigator Matthew Moneymaker speaks with two of the three witnesses and calls the report legit. Using the powerline poles as a gauge from about 1,530 feet away, he puts the figure at eight feet or more. It was a windy day, and the family thinks the wind covered the sound of their truck. Tishomingo National Wildlife Refuge sits about five miles to the northwest.

Source: https://www.bfro.net/GDB/show_report.asp?id=79845

Have you heard of Goliath's brothers?

Top 5 things to know about the other giants of Gath:

1) First Samuel seventeen makes Goliath of Gath famous, but Second Samuel twenty-one lists more Philistine champions tied to the same giant line, the descendants of Rapha.

2) Ishbi-benob threatens David in battle and is killed by Abishai after raising a new sword of impressive weight.

3) Another giant, Saph or Sippai, falls to Sibbecai the Hushathite in the same war cycle.

4) First Chronicles twenty says Elhanan son of Jair kills Lahmi, the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear is compared to a weaver's beam.

5) The chapter closes with a six-fingered, six-toed giant of Gath whom Jonathan son of Shimei strikes down, rounding out a cluster of oversized warriors around David's later wars.

Learn more: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=2%20Samuel%2021%3A15-22&version=NIV

posts.text:
Have you heard of Tahoe Tessie?

Top 5 things to know about Lake Tahoe's lake monster:

1) Tahoe Tessie is the popular name for a large serpent-like or humped creature reported in Lake Tahoe on the California-Nevada border.

2) Nineteenth-century settler accounts of a lake serpent appear by the mid-eighteen hundreds, including a widely repeated eighteen sixty-five report tied to I.C. Coggin.

3) Modern sightings describe dark shapes, multiple humps, and odd wakes on the deep alpine lake, including a nineteen eighty-two report credited to two Reno police officers.

4) Local writer Bob McCormick helped popularize the friendly "Tessie" nickname in the nineteen seventies and eighties through children's books and tourism chatter.

5) No specimen has been produced. Proposed ordinary explanations include large fish such as sturgeon, boat wakes, wind rows, floating debris, and optical tricks on cold clear water.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tahoe_Tessie
posts.headline: Have you heard of Tahoe Tessie?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Jersey Devil?

Top 5 things to know about the Pine Barrens legend:

1) The Jersey Devil is New Jersey's most famous cryptid, tied to the Pine Barrens and especially the Leeds Point area of Atlantic County.

2) Folklore says Mother Leeds bore a cursed thirteenth child in 1735 that became a winged, hooved creature and fled into the pines, though historians treat that birth story as legend rather than proven fact.

3) In January 1909 a media-driven flap of tracks, sightings, school closures, and posses swept South Jersey and Philadelphia, cementing the modern name Jersey Devil.

4) A "captured" specimen displayed at a Philadelphia dime museum turned out to be a kangaroo dressed with fake wings, a publicity stunt later tied to showman Norman Jeffries.

5) The creature remains a state mascot of sorts, from sports nicknames to roadside lore, even as reports stay scattered and physical evidence stays missing.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey_Devil
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Jersey Devil?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Zamzummim?

Top 5 things to know about this biblical giant people:

1) The Zamzummim appear in Deuteronomy 2 as an earlier people of the land later held by the Ammonites east of the Jordan.

2) The text says that land was also considered a land of the Rephaim, but the Ammonites called them Zamzummites or Zamzummim.

3) They are described as strong, numerous, and as tall as the Anakim, the same giant reputation attached to other Rephaim groups.

4) Deuteronomy says the Lord destroyed them before the Ammonites, who then drove them out and settled in their place.

5) Many readers connect them with the Zuzim named in Genesis 14 among the peoples struck by Chedorlaomer's coalition, though that link stays partly conjectural.

Learn more: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Deuteronomy%202%3A20-21&version=NIV
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Zamzummim?

posts.text:
Have you heard of Ogopogo?

Top 5 things to know about Canada's famous lake monster:

1) Ogopogo is the colonial name for a lake creature reported in Okanagan Lake, British Columbia, a deep freshwater fjord more than seventy miles long.

2) Syilx and Secwepemc traditions speak of n̓x̌ax̌aitkʷ or Naitaka, a powerful water being tied to places like Rattlesnake Island, long before the music-hall nickname stuck in the nineteen twenties.

3) Settler reports go back at least to Susan Allison in 1872, with later claims of a dark serpentine body thicker than a telephone pole and up to about fifty feet long.

4) Art Folden's 1968 home movie of a large wake, plus later beach and video sightings, kept the story in Canadian and international media.

5) Skeptics usually point to otters in a line, beavers, waterfowl, logs, or lake waves, while local tourism and First Nations voices still treat the lake spirit as part of the valley's identity.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogopogo
posts.headline: Have you heard of Ogopogo?

Answer: C) Hodag

The Hodag is Rhinelander, Wisconsin's famous lumber-camp monster, described with a frog-like head, elephantine grin, thick clawed legs, a spined dinosaur back, and a spear-tipped tail. In 1893 surveyor and prankster Eugene Shepard claimed he had killed one with dynamite, then in 1896 exhibited a "live" Hodag at the Oneida County Fair before admitting the carved-and-wired hoax when Smithsonian interest loomed. The creature stuck anyway as the town's mascot.

How'd you do?

Phoenix and the Valley of the Sun, Arizona, with reports stretching from Nevada into southern Arizona. March 13, 1997.

Between about 7:30 and 10:30 p.m. Mountain Standard Time, thousands of people watch lights move across roughly three hundred miles of sky. Early witnesses describe a huge V or carpenter's-square formation of lights, some saying the lights sit in a dark craft the size of a city block as it drifts silently toward Phoenix Sky Harbor. Actor and pilot Kurt Russell is among those who report the lights to air traffic control.

Around 10 p.m. a second event lights the southwest sky: a row of brilliant stationary or slowly descending orbs over the Sierra Estrella range, captured on countless home videos. Years later, then-governor Fife Symington says he saw something otherworldly that night and kept quiet so he would not panic people.

The Air National Guard and skeptics later tie the early formation to A-10 jets on an Operation Snowbird corridor and the 10 p.m. orbs to illumination flares dropped on the Barry Goldwater Range. Plenty of witnesses still say what they saw was no ordinary flight. One of the most watched nights in American UFO history still will not settle.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Lights

posts.text:
Fletchertown Road near Old Bowie, Prince George's County, Maryland. Fall of 1971.

Local folklore already whispered about a six-foot half-man, half-goat that walked on hooves, squealed before it struck, and haunted back roads and bridges. In spring 1971 a University of Maryland student collected Goatman legends around Clinton for a folklore class. That October, Prince George's County News journalist Karen Hosler pulled the archive material into a Halloween article that planted the beast firmly in Bowie.

Days later, April Edwards and friends John Hayden and Whillie Gheen hear strange noises near her house by the woods. Hayden says he sees a six-foot hairy animal walking on two feet. The next morning Edwards' puppy, Ginger, is gone. The family searches near Fletchertown Road by the Penn Central railroad and finds the dog decapitated. Hosler follows with a second headline tying residents' fear to the Goatman. By late November the Washington Post sends a reporter into the same remote woods.

Whether hermit, mad-scientist tall tale, or something that really walked those trees, the 1971 flap locked the Goatman into Maryland memory. Teens kept hunting him on Fletchertown Road for years after.

Source: https://boundarystones.weta.org/2023/10/27/goatman-prince-georges-county

posts.text:
Chester Castle, Cheshire, England. October 2025.

English Heritage motion-detecting cameras pick up unusual movement in the middle of the night at the locked compound. Staff are alerted. On the footage, a pale figure in dark clothing and a hood stands in front of the castle.

A security guard goes to investigate. The area is empty. His usually fearless dog refuses to enter. A full search of the locked grounds finds no intruder. The castle is protected by spikes on the battlements and additional cameras meant to catch anyone climbing the gates. Nobody is found.

English Heritage shares the still. Nearly half of staff across the charity's properties say they have witnessed something they could not explain, from spectral hands and vanishing soldier-like figures to piano music with no player. Curator Dr Michael Carter notes that chilling tales of the returning dead have been told since the dawn of recorded history, and that these new accounts keep the English ghost story tradition alive.

A hooded figure on castle CCTV. An empty courtyard. No tidy explanation.

Source: https://www.dailystar.co.uk/news/weird-news/ghostly-hooded-figure-caught-cctv-36127343
posts.headline: Chester Castle, Cheshire, England. October 2025.

Cody, Wyoming, looking west toward Cedar Mountain. Late September 2026.

Cody resident Jezriah Krubeck says nearly two dozen glowing orbs rose over the ridge every night from November through February, then vanished for months. Within the last two or three nights of the Cowboy State Daily report, he says they are back. From his porch he watches white orbs float up, move toward each other, and follow the ridgeline left to right.

He holds a doctorate in education and says he tried to disprove what he was seeing. Neighbors confirm the lights. He rules out stars, meteors, and ordinary cosmic events because the objects change direction, stop, and seem to react when he puts a laser on them. They do not match satellite trackers and lack the flashing beacons required on aircraft. He also notices conventional air traffic increasing dramatically once the orbs appear.

Wyoming Mutual UFO Network director Richard Beckwith reviews Krubeck's video and says it shows several glowing white orbs moving in different directions. He dismisses aircraft for missing navigation lights, and is inclined to dismiss drones and balloons. Right now, he says, he has no explanation for the objects recorded.

Silent lights over Cedar Mountain. No tidy answer attached.

Source: https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/09/25/mystery-orbs-are-back-over-cody-and-ufo-authority-cant-explain-them/

Near the Edge of the World trail area north of Sedona, Yavapai County, Arizona. June 15, 2025.

Three Rimrock residents, Amber, her husband, and his cousin, drive deep into the pines after hearing a missing camper is lost in the canyons. They spend hours shouting her name and sweeping the brush with a spotlight. Earlier in daylight, Amber hears two hard tree knocks while calling out and jokes that it must be Bigfoot.

After dark they light up something about seventy-five yards away. She describes a roughly seven-foot biped, at least four hundred pounds, with a wide body and shoulders, matted white and brown hair, a flat leathery face, and golden eye shine. It stares. They watch for one to two minutes, then leave as fast as they can. Her husband, a hunter and lifelong skeptic, says he knows wildlife and has no other explanation.

The missing hiker, Janelle Banda, is rescued after about two and a half days. She tells them something glowing moved toward her in the dark, which is what made her run and fall into the canyon. BFRO investigator Matthew Moneymaker interviews two of the witnesses by phone. The woods north of Sedona keep the rest of the story.

Source: https://www.bfro.net/GDB/show_report.asp?id=78863

Have you heard of the Grootslang?

Top 5 things to know about South Africa's great snake of the Richtersveld:

1) Grootslang means big snake in Afrikaans and Dutch, and the legend places it in a deep cave in the Richtersveld of South Africa.

2) Folklore describes a serpent forty to fifty feet long that leaves a track about three feet wide, sometimes said to guard diamonds in a Wonder Hole or Bottomless Pit.

3) Local stories link the cave to the sea or the Orange River and claim the pit holds gems funneled toward the current.

4) Prospecting lore includes the 1917 disappearance of English businessman Peter Grayson after a lion attack on his party, which locals tied to the creature.

5) Writers such as Lawrence G. Green argued the core tale grew from python sightings, with diamond eyes and impossible size added as storytelling.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grootslang
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Grootslang?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Nandi Bear?

Top 5 things to know about East Africa's sloping-backed cryptid:

1) The Nandi bear is a cryptid reported from western Kenya and nearby East African highlands, named for the Nandi people.

2) Descriptions paint a ferocious, powerfully built carnivore with high front shoulders over about four feet and a sloping back, sometimes said to stand on its hind legs.

3) Local names include Chemosit and Kerit; some accounts give it reddish hair and a reputation for attacking at night.

4) Sightings clustered in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, then thinned out, and no specimen was ever secured.

5) Zoologists generally treat reports as misidentified hyenas, honey badgers, or folklore, while older fringe ideas once floated extinct chalicotheres before that theory was dropped.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandi_Bear
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Nandi Bear?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Akkorokamui?

Top 5 things to know about Hokkaido's giant octopus spirit:

1) Akkorokamui is a gigantic octopus-like being from Ainu folklore said to lurk in Uchiura Bay, also called Funka Bay, in Hokkaido, Japan.

2) Traditional accounts put its body on a huge scale, sometimes described as covering about a hectare of water, with an intense red color visible from far off.

3) Folklore warns it can swallow ships, so crews watching for fish in those waters kept a gaff ready and steered clear when the redness showed.

4) One origin story says it began as a monstrous spider that ravaged a village before a sea god plunged it into the bay and transformed it into an octopus.

5) Related Ainu sea-monster traditions include other giant octopus names, and the figure later shows up in broader Japanese popular culture as a bay-lord yokai.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akkorokamui
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Akkorokamui?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Emim?

Top 5 things to know about the biblical giant people of Moab:

1) In the Hebrew Bible the Emim (or Emites) are named as an earlier people of Moab, remembered as great, numerous, and tall.

2) Deuteronomy 2 compares them to the Anakim and says they were also regarded as Rephaim, while the Moabites called them Emim.

3) Genesis 14:5 places them among the peoples defeated at Shaveh-kiriathaim by the coalition led by Chedorlaomer.

4) Tradition holds the Moabites later displaced them and occupied their land.

5) Rashi glosses the name as the dreaded ones, from a Hebrew root tied to horror or terror, which is why the label stuck in later reading.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emite
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Emim?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Emela-ntouka?

Top 5 things to know about the Congo Basin's reported elephant killer:

1) Emela-ntouka is a cryptid reported from swamp forests of the Republic of the Congo, especially the Likouala region north of the Equator.

2) Informants describe an elephant-sized semi-aquatic animal with a heavy tail and a single horn on the snout, feared for goring elephants.

3) French colonial hunting inspector Lucien Blancou published related forest-rhinoceros hearsay in the journal Mammalia in 1954, though he never recorded the local name.

4) American researcher Roy Mackal collected the name Emela-ntouka on 1980-81 Congo expeditions and published it in his 1987 book while searching for Mokele-mbembe.

5) Mackal floated a surviving ceratopsian idea, then set it aside and favored an unusual semi-aquatic rhinoceros; no specimen has ever been produced.

Learn more: https://enigmaatlas.com/cryptids/emela-ntouka
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Emela-ntouka?

The Sheepsquatch, often tied to older White Thing lore in West Virginia, is described as a large white woolly biped with horns, sharp teeth, and sometimes clawed hands, reported mainly in southwestern counties such as Boone, Kanawha, Putnam, and Mason. Folklorists trace early White Thing documentation to mid-century local accounts later collected in print, while hard physical evidence has never turned up.

How'd you do?

Rendlesham Forest, Suffolk, England, just outside RAF Woodbridge, then used by the United States Air Force. Late December 1980.

Around 3 a.m. on December 26, security personnel near the East Gate see lights descending into the pines and go out thinking it may be a crash. Deputy base commander Lieutenant Colonel Charles I. Halt later writes that they found a glowing metallic object with colored lights that moved through the trees while farm animals nearby went into a frenzy. Servicemen return after daybreak and report ground impressions, burn marks, and broken branches. Local police called to the scene say the only lights they can confirm are from the Orford Ness lighthouse miles away.

On the night of December 28 Halt leads another party, takes radiation readings around a triangle of depressions, and records the investigation on a microcassette as lights reappear. His January 13, 1981 memo to the UK Ministry of Defence becomes the backbone of what the British press later calls Britain's Roswell. The MoD says it was never a security threat. Skeptics point to a fireball, the lighthouse, and bright stars. The airmen who were there still tell a different story.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rendlesham_Forest_incident

posts.text:
The former province of Gévaudan in south-central France, modern Lozère and Haute-Loire. Summer of 1764.

In early June a young woman tending cattle in the Mercoire Forest near Langogne is rushed by an animal she later describes as like a wolf, yet not a wolf. The herd drives it off. Then on June 30, fourteen-year-old Jeanne Boulet is killed near Les Hubacs. Her burial record names the ferocious beast.

Over the next three years the attacks spread across roughly ninety by eighty kilometers. Period estimates put more than two hundred attacks and about one hundred deaths, many victims partly eaten, often with the throat torn out. Witnesses describe a tawny or russet animal with a dark stripe, a long tufted tail, calf-sized or larger, capable of huge bounds. King Louis XV sends dragoons and royal hunters. Wolves are shot and displayed. The killings continue until local hunter Jean Chastel brings down a large wolf-like animal at Mont Mouchet on June 19, 1767, and the wave finally stops.

Historians still argue wolf, wolfdog, hyena, or something never cleanly identified. The countryside remembers a beast.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beast_of_Gevaudan
posts.headline: The former province of Gévaudan in south-central France, modern Lozère and Haute-Loire. Summer of 1764.

posts.text:
30 East Drive, Pontefract, West Yorkshire, England. December 16, 2025.

The semi-detached house has a reputation going back to 1966, when Jean and Joe Pritchard moved in with their children and reported years of violent activity: lights cutting out, green foam from taps, photographs slashed, family members slapped and pushed on the stairs. Locals and later visitors tied it to a tall black-cloaked hooded figure nicknamed the Black Monk. Current owner Bil Bungay says he is too scared to spend a night there and rents it to investigators and horror tourists.

Merseyside paranormal team Heavy Metal Haunting, led by John Wharton, books a seventy-one hour stay. Wharton says he arrived skeptical. Live on TikTok they claim lights flickering, light sensors that will not stop, and a figure moving on the stairs. He tells the Liverpool Echo he does not think they met the Black Monk, but that they definitely encountered something, and that the land under the house may be the real problem.

Seventy-one hours. One of England's most infamous addresses. The cameras keep rolling. The house still will not quiet down.

Source: https://www.liverpoolecho.co.uk/news/liverpool-news/71-hours-most-haunted-house-33319236
posts.headline: 30 East Drive, Pontefract, West Yorkshire, England. December 16, 2025.

Centralia, Illinois. Friday, August 28, 2026, about 5:30 a.m., after the full moon lunar eclipse.

A local sky-watcher is walking the dog with a companion when she notices what look like three very bright stars in a triangle to the south. She watches a few seconds, then realizes all three are slowly moving southward together. They are lights, not stars.

She snaps a night-mode phone photo with a three-second shutter, then records about twenty seconds of video. In the footage a faint dark triangle seems to carry the three lights, the brightest at the top, before the object fades from view. She hears no sound. She lives within roughly sixty miles of Scott Air Force Base and says she has never seen anything like it.

The account is filed with NUFORC and picked up by local coverage. A silent triangle the size of a field over southern Illinois. No official explanation attached.

Source: https://101theeagle.com/centralia-illinois-triangle-lights/
posts.headline: Centralia, Illinois. Friday, August 28, 2026, about 5:30 a.m., after the full moon lunar eclipse.

Near Lost Valley Reservoir in Payette National Forest, Adams County, Idaho, about sixteen miles northwest of McCall. Memorial Day weekend, May 22 to 25, 2026.

A group of about ten teens from Parma is camping in a secluded opening off Lost Valley Road. Friday night one of them sees a tall dark figure a few yards behind a tent and says nothing until Monday. Saturday, while someone searches the tree line for a friend, something walks with her and whistles from different directions. Sunday around three in the morning another camper hears aggressive rhythmic knocking and writes it off as a woodpecker.

Later Sunday, one of the guys heading for the makeshift bathroom sees a roughly nine-foot biped with dark fur and blank reflective eyes walking toward him. He grabs a .22. Several of them push into the woods and say three or more creatures circle them, hide behind trees, and try to separate the group. One camper says he fires at one of them, then fires warning shots. By morning they find handprints on vehicle windows, broken trees arranged in a wide circle near a neighboring camp, and what look like prints and nests around their own site.

BFRO investigator Matthew Moneymaker interviews witnesses, rates the report, and notes four daylight visual sightings among the group. The woods do not offer a tidy ending.

Source: https://www.bfro.net/GDB/show_report.asp?id=81202

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Tengu?

Top 5 things to know about Japan's mountain goblins:

1) Tengu are legendary creatures in Japanese folk religion, classed among yōkai or kami, whose name literally means heavenly dog.

2) Early art shows them as kite-like birds of prey that can take human form; later images settle on the red-faced long-nosed mountain figure most people recognize today.

3) Buddhist writers long treated tengu as disruptive demons and omens of war before the image softened into dangerous but sometimes protective forest spirits.

4) They are closely tied to Shugendō mountain asceticism and are often drawn wearing the garb of yamabushi monks.

5) Folklore places them in deep mountains and forests across Japan, where they may abduct, teach, or punish travelers who show arrogance in sacred places.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tengu
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Tengu?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Manananggal?

Top 5 things to know about the Philippine self-segmenting night hunter:

1) The manananggal is a creature from Philippine folklore, especially strong in the Visayas, whose name comes from a word meaning to remove or separate.

2) At night it is said to detach its upper torso, sprout bat-like wings, and leave its lower half behind while it hunts.

3) Folklore says it preys on sleeping pregnant women and the unborn, using a long tongue-like appendage, and is also linked to attacks on lovers and newborns.

4) The abandoned lower torso is the weak point; salt, garlic, ash, or fire can keep the halves from rejoining, and sunrise without reunion means death.

5) Spanish colonial writers already recorded related magtatangal stories in the late 1500s, and the figure remains a staple of Filipino horror film and festival lore.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manananggal

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Dobhar-chú?

Top 5 things to know about Ireland's King Otter:

1) The Dobhar-chú, whose name means water hound or water dog in Irish, is a cryptid from Irish and Scottish folklore said to live in lakes and rivers.

2) Descriptions mix otter and hound, sometimes half dog and half fish, with accounts putting it many times larger than a normal otter.

3) The most famous legend ties to Glenade Lough in County Leitrim in 1722, where Grace McGloighlin is said to have been killed by the creature.

4) A carved headstone in Conwall Cemetery near Glenade depicts a strange animal and is traditionally linked to that story.

5) Modern claims continue; in 2003 artist Sean Corcoran and his wife reported a large dark fast-swimming creature with orange flipper-like feet off Omey Island in Connemara.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobhar-ch%C3%BA

Have you heard of the Rephaim?

Top 5 things to know about the biblical giant people and the shades of the dead:

1) In the Hebrew Bible, Rephaim can mean a people of unusual height and stature, named in Deuteronomy among the ancient inhabitants of the land.

2) King Og of Bashan is the most famous Rephaite in the conquest stories, remembered as the last of his kind in that region.

3) Other giant groups in the same narrative world include the Anakim, Emim, and Zamzummim, often linked together in later reading.

4) The same word also names the weak or departed spirits in Sheol in passages like Isaiah, Psalms, and Proverbs, so the label carries a double life.

5) Outside Israel, related Northwest Semitic texts from Ugarit speak of rpum figures tied to dead kings and heroes, which scholars compare with the biblical usage.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rephaite
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Rephaim?

Have you heard of the Skunk Ape?

Top 5 things to know about Florida's swamp-dwelling cousin of Bigfoot:

1) The Skunk Ape is a large, hairy bipedal cryptid reported across the southeastern United States, especially Florida's Everglades and Big Cypress.

2) Witnesses usually put it around five to seven feet tall with mottled reddish-brown hair, often smaller than classic Pacific Northwest Bigfoot descriptions.

3) It is named for a foul odor witnesses compare to a skunk, which shows up again and again in reports.

4) Sightings clustered hard from the 1950s through the 1970s, including Broward County waves, Palm Beach deputy encounters, and later Everglades tour-operator claims.

5) Mainstream science treats it as folklore, misidentification, or hoax; the National Park Service has called it a hoax, while Florida culture still keeps the legend alive on signs, tours, and conferences.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skunk_ape
